title: Part 1, Chapter 5
paragraphs: In which the story of our knight's mishap is continued

Finding, then, that he really could not move, he hit upon his usual remedy, which was to think of some passage from his books, and his craze brought to mind the story of Baldwin and the Marquis of Mantua, when Carloto left him wounded on the mountainside — a tale known by heart by every child, not forgotten by the young men, and praised and even believed by the old folk, and for all that no whit truer than the miracles of Mahomet. This seemed to him a perfect fit for the case he was in, so, making a show of severe suffering, he began to roll on the ground and to gasp out the very words the wounded knight of the wood is said to have spoken:
Where art thou, lady mine, that thou My sorrow dost not rue? Thou canst not know it, lady mine, Or else thou art untrue.
And so he went on with the ballad as far as the lines:
O noble Marquis of Mantua, My Uncle and liege lord!

As luck would have it, when he had got this far, there happened along a peasant from his own village, a neighbour of his, who had been to the mill with a load of wheat; and seeing the man stretched there, he came up and asked him who he was and what was the matter that he was groaning so pitifully.

Don Quixote was firmly convinced that this was the Marquis of Mantua, his uncle, so the only reply he made was to keep going with his ballad, telling the tale of his misfortune and of the loves of the Emperor's son and his wife, exactly as the ballad sings it.

The peasant stood astonished at hearing such nonsense, and relieving him of the visor (already battered to pieces by blows), he wiped his face, which was covered with dust; and as soon as he had done so he recognised him and said, "Señor Quixada" (which seems to have been what he was called when he was in his senses and hadn't yet changed from a quiet country gentleman into a knight-errant), "who has brought your worship to this state?" But to every question the other only kept going with his ballad.

Seeing this, the good man removed as best he could his breastplate and backpiece, to see if he had any wound, but could see no blood nor any mark of any kind. He then managed to lift him off the ground, and with no little effort hoisted him onto his ass, which seemed to him the easier mount; and gathering up the arms — even the splinters of the lance — he tied them on Rocinante, and leading Rocinante by the bridle and the ass by the halter, he took the road for the village, very sad at having to listen to the absurd stuff Don Quixote was talking.

Nor was Don Quixote less sad, for what with blows and bruises he could not sit upright on the ass, and from time to time he sent up sighs to heaven loud enough that the peasant had to ask once more what ailed him. And it can only have been the devil himself who put into his head tales to match his own adventures, for now, forgetting Baldwin, he thought of the Moor Abindarraez, when the Alcaide of Antequera, Rodrigo de Narvaez, took him prisoner and carried him off to his castle; so when the peasant asked him again how he was and what ailed him, he replied with the very words and phrases that the captive Abindarraez had used to Rodrigo de Narvaez, exactly as he had read the story in Jorge de Montemayor's "Diana" — applying it to his own situation so neatly that the peasant went along cursing his fate for having to listen to such a load of nonsense. From it, however, he concluded that his neighbour was mad, and pressed on as fast as he could to the village to escape the wearisomeness of Don Quixote's harangue, who, at the end of it, said, "Señor Don Rodrigo de Narvaez, you should know that the fair Xarifa I have mentioned is now the lovely Dulcinea del Toboso, for whom I have done, am doing, and will do the most famous deeds of chivalry that this world has seen, is to see, or ever shall see."

To this the peasant answered, "Señor — sinner that I am! — can your worship not see that I'm not Don Rodrigo de Narvaez nor the Marquis of Mantua, but Pedro Alonso your neighbour, and that your worship is neither Baldwin nor Abindarraez, but the worthy gentleman Señor Quixada?"

"I know who I am," replied Don Quixote, "and I know that I may be not only those I have named, but all the Twelve Peers of France, and even all the Nine Worthies, since my achievements outdo everything they have done — all of them together, and each of them on his own."

With this kind of talk and more like it, they reached the village just as night was beginning to fall, but the peasant waited until it was a little later, so the battered gentleman wouldn't be seen riding in such a miserable state. When the time seemed right to him he entered the village and made for Don Quixote's house, which he found all in confusion. The curate and the village barber, who were great friends of Don Quixote, were there, and his housekeeper was saying to them loudly, "What does your worship think can have happened to my master, Señor Licentiate Pero Perez?" — for so the curate was called. "It is three days now since we've seen anything of him, or the hack, or the buckler, lance, or armour. Wretch that I am! I am certain of it — as sure as I was born to die — that these accursed books of chivalry he has, and has got into the habit of reading constantly, have unhinged his reason; for now I remember many times hearing him say to himself that he meant to turn knight-errant and go all over the world in search of adventures. To the devil and Barabbas with such books, that have ruined in this way the finest mind there was in all La Mancha!"

The niece said the same, and more: "You should know, Master Nicholas" — for that was the barber's name — "it was often my uncle's way to spend two days and nights together poring over those unholy books of misadventures, after which he would fling the book away, snatch up his sword, and fall to slashing the walls; and when he was worn out he would say he had killed four giants like four towers; and the sweat that ran off him when he was exhausted he said was the blood of the wounds he had received in battle. Then he would drink a great jug of cold water and become calm and quiet, saying this water was a most precious potion brought to him by the sage Esquife, a great magician and friend of his. But I take all the blame on myself for never telling your worships of my uncle's vagaries, that you might have put a stop to them before things came to this pass, and burnt all these accursed books — and there are many of them — that richly deserve to be burnt like heretics."

"I say the same," said the curate, "and by my faith tomorrow shall not pass without public judgment on them, and may they be condemned to the flames so they do not lead any other reader to behave as my good friend seems to have behaved."

All this the peasant overheard, and from it he finally grasped what was wrong with his neighbour, so he began calling aloud, "Open, your worships, to Señor Baldwin and to Señor the Marquis of Mantua, who comes badly wounded; and to Señor Abindarraez, the Moor, whom the valiant Rodrigo de Narvaez, the Alcaide of Antequera, brings captive."
At these words they all hurried out, and when they recognised their friend, master, and uncle, who had not yet dismounted from the ass because he couldn't, they ran to embrace him.
"Stop!" he said; "for I am badly wounded through my horse's fault. Carry me to bed, and if possible send for the wise Urganda to look at my wounds and cure them."

"There you go! plague on it!" cried the housekeeper at this. "Didn't my heart tell the truth as to which foot my master was lame of? Off to bed with your worship at once, and we'll contrive to cure you here without fetching any Hurgada. A curse, I say, once more, and a hundred times more, on those books of chivalry that have brought your worship to such a pass."

They carried him to bed at once, and after searching for his wounds could find none, but he said they were all bruises from a heavy fall with his horse Rocinante while in combat with ten giants, the biggest and boldest on earth.
"So, so!" said the curate. "Are there giants in the dance? By the sign of the Cross I will burn them tomorrow before the day is over."

They put a host of questions to Don Quixote, but his only answer to any of them was to give him something to eat and let him sleep, for that was what he needed most. They did so, and the curate questioned the peasant at length about how he had found Don Quixote. He told him, and the nonsense Don Quixote had spouted both when found and on the road home, all of which only made the licentiate the more eager to do what he did the next day — which was to summon his friend the barber, Master Nicholas, and go with him to Don Quixote's house.
